system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
mechanism: Ask-Tell-Ask structures information exchange by first asking what the patient already understands or wants to know, then telling the key information briefly and without jargon, and finally asking again to assess what the patient absorbed and whether the patient is ready to proceed. The structure avoids a one-way information dump and permits the clinician to tailor the amount and complexity of information.
vignette: A physician is about to explain a newly confirmed but nonurgent diagnosis to an adult patient during a follow-up visit. The patient is alert, has decision-making capacity, speaks the same language as the physician, and has not expressed a preference to avoid medical information. The physician wants to use a patient-centered strategy that both tailors the explanation to the patient's starting knowledge and checks how the information was received.
lead: Which of the following approaches best accomplishes this goal?
correct: First ask what the patient understands about the condition, then give the main information briefly in plain language, and then ask what the patient took away and whether the patient is ready to discuss next steps
distractors: Give a comprehensive explanation of the diagnosis and all treatment options before asking any questions so that the patient receives the complete medical picture
Begin by asking the patient to choose a treatment before providing diagnostic information so that the clinician does not influence the decision
Ask a family member what the patient understands, provide the explanation to the family member, and let the family decide how much information to relay
Provide the diagnosis using standard medical terminology and ask at the end whether the patient has any questions
distractor_notes: A long one-way information dump does not tailor information to the patient's baseline understanding and can overwhelm comprehension.
Shared decision making requires relevant information before treatment choices can be meaningfully weighed; asking for a treatment choice before explaining the diagnosis reverses that sequence.
A capable adult patient is the primary participant in the communication unless the patient requests family involvement; routine substitution of a family member is inappropriate.
Medical jargon and a generic invitation for questions do not provide the iterative assessment and tailoring built into Ask-Tell-Ask.
key_expl: Ask-Tell-Ask begins by eliciting the patient's current understanding, goals, values, or permission to receive information. The clinician then gives the central message briefly and without jargon. The second Ask checks whether the patient has heard and absorbed the information and whether the conversation can move forward. The key therefore describes the full iterative sequence rather than a one-way lecture, premature treatment choice, surrogate substitution, or jargon-heavy explanation.
objective: Use Ask-Tell-Ask to tailor information to a patient's baseline understanding, communicate the main message clearly, and reassess how the information was received before continuing.
clues: goal includes checking how information was received

sources.title: Communication in Cancer Care (PDQ®)–Health Professional Version
sources.support: NCI describes Ask-Tell-Ask as a three-step strategy: first ask to elicit understanding, goals, values, or permission; tell the main message briefly without jargon; then ask again to ensure the patient has heard and absorbed the information and is ready to move on.
